newsitem.title: USA: U.S. probes Calif. law schools' student admissions.
newsitem.headline: U.S. probes Calif. law schools' student admissions.

text.p: The U.S. Department of Education said on Tuesday it had launched a probe of whether the student admissions policies of three University of California law schools were racially discriminatory.

The department said it opened the investigation in response to a complaint filed in March by six civil rights groups alleging that the university discriminated against minorities and women in admission to graduate schools.

In a letter to University of California President Richard Atkinson sent last Friday, the department's Office for Civil Rights said it would investigate whether the admissions policies of the university's Berkeley, Davis and Los Angeles law schools discriminated on the basis of race.
The department said it would not investigate whether the law schools discriminated against women.

"As admissions data for the 1997-98 school year become available for other graduate and professional schools, the Office for Civil Rights may identify additional schools for investigation," the letter said.

The student admissions policies of the huge, nine-campus University of California have been surrounded by controversy ever since the university's governing Board of Regents voted in 1995 to scrap racial preferences in student admissions.
The new admissions policy takes effect for the law schools and other graduate programmes this fall. For undergraduates, the new policy takes effect from the spring of 1998.
The three law schools have said they expect a sharp drop in the number of minority students enrolling this fall.
Affirmative action supporters said the admissions figures confirmed their worst fears about the effects of the change in admissions policy.

The Department of Education can investigate complaints of discrimination in educational programmes that receive federal aid. It can cut off the federal aid if the institution is found to discriminate and does nothing to remedy it.
The University of California receives more than $1 billion a year in federal aid.

But Department of Education spokesman Rodger Murphey said it was very rare for funds to be cut. If an institution was found to discriminate, a plan was usually put in place to bring it into compliance with the law, he said.
He said an average complaint takes about 125 days to investigate but this one might take longer.
University of California spokesman Terry Lightfoot said the university would help the Department of Education with its inquiry.

He said the university had no intention of reducing its commitment to diversity. "It's our intent to continue to work to improve the numbers of minorities enrolled in the university through a variety of outreach programmes," he said.

The chief architect of the University of California's new admissions policy was Ward Connerly, a regent. Connerly later led the campaign for a statewide ballot measure abolishing affirmative action programmes in state government that was passed by California voters last November.
